clue.text: Brave, violent dance

definitions.meaning: a Brave is a Native American warrior, and this tribe is a famous example
the Parisian street dance of the early 1900s mimicking a rough quarrel between a man and a woman

explanation.surface: A courageous person performing a fierce dance.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a Native American people famed as warriors; the other is a showy Parisian dance acting out a brutal fight.

clue.text: His parlour inspired 3's irregular ode

parts.note: Coleridge (3-down) wrote his irregular ode 'Songs of the' little folk after visiting a Devon cave known as their parlour

explanation.surface: Someone's sitting room gave a poet the idea for an ode.
explanation.walkthrough: '3' points to the answer at 3-down, the poet Coleridge; his 'Songs of the Pixies' was set in a sandstone cave near Ottery St Mary called the Pixies' Parlour.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairy-like sprite of West Country folklore, whose cave Coleridge celebrated in verse.

clue.text: Poet portrays old king at a high point

parts.note: Old King Cole is the merry old soul of the nursery rhyme
a ridge is a raised crest of land

explanation.surface: A poem depicts an ancient monarch standing on a summit.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romantic writer of 'Kubla Khan' and 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner'.

clue.text: Guildford girl from Shalott?

parts.note: Malory places Astolat at Guildford, and Tennyson's Lady of Shalott is the Arthurian maid of Astolat

explanation.surface: A young woman from a Surrey town who seems to come from a legendary place.
explanation.walkthrough: Guildford is a town in Surrey; Malory identified it with Astolat, home of the maid who loved Lancelot, whom Tennyson recast as the Lady of Shalott.
explanation.definitionFit: The fair maid of Astolat in Arthurian legend, the figure behind Tennyson's Lady of Shalott.

clue.text: Pun for a drama without music?

definitions.meaning: a pun is a joke exploiting double meanings of a term
a stage piece made only of spoken text, as opposed to an opera or musical

explanation.surface: Asking whether a joke might stand in for a straight theatre piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Witty verbal games include puns; read as two words it is a spoken stage piece with no songs.

clue.text: A good, fitting row upset amusing play

indicators.note: upset tells us these words are knocked over and reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: A good and fitting quarrel disrupts a comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges the fifteen letters of A GOOD FITTING ROW.
explanation.definitionFit: Beckett's tragicomedy of two tramps waiting for someone who never comes is famously funny as well as bleak.

clue.text: Edison's outlaw might be aged Rene

indicators.note: might be suggests the letters of these two words could be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: An outlaw in a story could turn out to be an elderly man called Rene.
explanation.definitionFit: A turncoat who has deserted a cause and lives beyond the law.

clue.text: Ad discreet look, say, into grotesque fantasist

indicators.note: say signals that the word for the glance is spoken, giving a name pronounced the same way

parts.note: a peek is a quick, furtive glance

explanation.surface: A sly glance into the mind of a writer of the weird.
explanation.walkthrough: Mervyn Peake wrote the Gormenghast novels, full of grotesque figures; his surname is pronounced like PEEK.
explanation.definitionFit: Mervyn Peake, author of the Gormenghast trilogy, was a writer and illustrator of gothic, grotesque fantasy.

clue.text: French nobleman let slip philosopher

parts.note: aristo is the informal word for an aristocrat, used of French nobles in the Revolution

indicators.note: slip suggests the letters of the word let slide out of order

explanation.surface: An aristocrat from France accidentally revealed a thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'let slip' reads as 'revealed', but 'slip' shuffles LET into TLE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek thinker who studied under Plato and tutored Alexander.

clue.text: Pound provides several examples of such rejoicing

definitions.text: Pound provides several examples of such rejoicing

parts.words: Pound provides several examples of such rejoicing
parts.note: Ezra Pound used the word as a title, and the collective term for a flock of larks names a joyful uplift

explanation.surface: A poet supplies many instances of celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' looks like money or a blow but is Ezra Pound, author of a poem with this title; 'an exaltation of larks' is also the collective noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Elation and lofty joy; the same term is the collective noun for a flock of larks.

clue.text: Novelist of musketeer seen with missing artist

indicators.note: missing tells us the artist's letters are absent from the musketeer's name

parts.note: Aramis is one of the Three Musketeers in Dumas
RA stands for Royal Academician, a crossword artist

explanation.surface: A writer of a swashbuckler appears alongside a painter who has gone astray.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley or Martin, the father and son who both wrote celebrated British fiction.

clue.text: Ziegler involved with new composer

indicators.note: involved suggests the letters are tangled up together into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A person called Ziegler takes part with a fresh music writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Legrenzi was a seventeenth-century Venetian writer of operas and church music.

clue.text: Alexander and Catherine may be modern or classical

definitions.meaning: both rulers carry the epithet 'the Great'
at Oxford, the classics degree is so called and PPE is its modern counterpart

explanation.surface: Two famous rulers might be thought of as either contemporary or ancient.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford's degree in classics is nicknamed Greats, and Philosophy, Politics and Economics is Modern Greats.
explanation.definitionFit: Famous monarchs styled 'the Great'; also Oxford slang for its final honours school in classics, with a modern version.

clue.text: Booklovers beware — new dues for what's secondhand

indicators.note: new signals that the word dues is formed afresh from its letters

explanation.surface: A warning to book collectors about fresh charges on preowned volumes.
explanation.definitionFit: Something previously owned, like a book from a charity shop, is not fresh from the shop.

clue.text: Trial acts rewritten for composer

indicators.note: rewritten tells us these words are reworded into a new letter order

explanation.surface: The scenes of a courtroom drama are redrafted for a musician.
explanation.definitionFit: Domenico Scarlatti, Italian Baroque keyboard writer, or his father Alessandro.

clue.text: Some poems of Heine

parts.note: the German word for poems, as used for collections of verse by Heine

explanation.surface: A handful of verses by a German poet.
explanation.definitionFit: The German term for poems, the title of Heine's collected verse.

clue.text: Gamekeeper's friend as Lady of the Lake?

definitions.meaning: Lady Chatterley, lover of the gamekeeper Mellors in Lawrence's novel
a lady whose name is also that of the large lake bordering Germany, Austria and Switzerland

explanation.surface: Someone friendly with a gamekeeper is cast as the Arthurian lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lady of the Lake' suggests Arthur's enchantress, but it means a woman named after the Bodensee.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Chatterley's first name; the same word names the Bodensee in English.

clue.text: Moravia's cloistered adolescent gains too, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that gains too may be only one arrangement of these letters

explanation.surface: A sheltered teenager in an Italian novel also benefits.
explanation.definitionFit: Title hero of Alberto Moravia's 1944 novella about a sheltered boy's coming of age.

clue.text: Borrow story from travelling man

parts.note: George Borrow's semi-autobiographical tale of wanderings among the Romany, titled with their word for a philologist

explanation.surface: Take a tale on loan from a wanderer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Borrow' looks like a verb but is George Borrow, Victorian author of travel books about Gypsy life.
explanation.definitionFit: George Borrow's 1851 novel of his wandering youth among the Romany people.

clue.text: Necessity in fine edition

indicators.note: in shows the letters sit inside the phrase fine edition

explanation.surface: Something essential found in a quality printing.
explanation.definitionFit: A requirement or something one cannot do without.

clue.text: Trollope's candidate for Scottish town

definitions.meaning: Gustavus ... stands for Parliament in Trollope's Doctor Thorne

explanation.surface: A Victorian novelist's choice for a place in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A parliamentary hopeful in Trollope's Barsetshire novel; also a small burgh in the Scottish Borders region.

clue.text: Michael Frayn's take on Aristophanes take on Socrates?

definitions.text: Michael Frayn's take on Aristophanes take on Socrates?

parts.words: Michael Frayn's take on Aristophanes take on Socrates?
parts.note: Aristophanes mocked Socrates in a comedy, and Frayn gave a later play of his the same title

explanation.surface: Wondering how a modern playwright reworks an ancient satire of a philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Aristophanes' comedy mocking Socrates, reused by Michael Frayn for a play.

clue.text: Partridge spoke of it in English and also spelled it with a b

definitions.text: Partridge spoke of it in English and also spelled it with a b

parts.words: Partridge spoke of it in English and also spelled it with a b
parts.note: Eric Partridge's guide pairs a word with itself prefixed by 'ab', a and b in front

explanation.surface: A game bird talked about something in English and spelt it with an extra letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partridge' is Eric Partridge, lexicographer, whose book is 'Usage and Abusage'; with 'a b' in front the answer becomes the second title word.
explanation.definitionFit: Customary practice in language, the subject of Eric Partridge's guide.

clue.text: Discreet movements of Figes characters

parts.note: silent drifting like a spectre, the title of a novel by Eva Figes

explanation.surface: Characters in a novel move quietly.
explanation.definitionFit: Gliding unnoticed like a phantom; also the title of Eva Figes's 1988 novel.

clue.text: Dostoevsky's jottings on the Tube?

parts.note: the London Tube is the Underground, and Dostoevsky wrote jottings from underground

explanation.surface: A Russian novelist scribbling on a London train.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tube is London's Underground railway, pointing to 'Notes from Underground'.
explanation.definitionFit: Brief written jottings, as in the title of Dostoevsky's novella from underground.

clue.text: Colonnade fronting some temples of Athens

indicators.note: fronting points to the letters at the front of each of the following words

explanation.surface: A row of columns standing before some of the shrines of Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: A roofed portico of pillars in ancient Greek architecture.

clue.text: Vague sort of article, frequently appearing

definitions.meaning: the grammatical article 'a' or 'an', among the commonest words in English

explanation.surface: A hazy kind of newspaper piece that crops up often.
explanation.definitionFit: Imprecise or unspecified; in grammar, 'a' and 'an' make up this kind of article.

clue.text: Ballantyne's rescuer albeit of new design

indicators.note: new design tells us these letters are laid out in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A Victorian author's saviour, though reworked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of new design' reads as one phrase, but 'of' is fodder: 'new design' rearranges ALBEIT OF. R. M. Ballantyne wrote 'The Lifeboat'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea rescue vessel, the subject of R. M. Ballantyne's boys' adventure novel.

clue.text: The first believer in God

parts.note: first is abbreviated 1st, with the digit one read as I

explanation.surface: The original person of faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who holds that a deity exists.
